alternates.speaker: Tulsidas (narrating)
alternates.setting: After Ram leaves for the forest, his mother Kausalya keeps his childhood things.
alternates.sanskrit: जननी निरखति बान-धनुहियाँ। बार-बार उर नैननि लावति प्रभुजूकी ललित पनहियाँ॥ कबहुँ प्रथम ज्यों जाइ जगावति कहि प्रिय बचन सँवारे। उठहु तात! बलि मातु बदनपर, अनुज-सखा सब द्वारे॥
alternates.line: She held his little shoes to her heart, and some mornings still went to wake him.
alternates.translation: The mother gazes at his little bow and arrows. Again and again she presses the Lord's small, lovely shoes to her heart and eyes. Sometimes, as before, she goes to wake him with tender words: "Get up, my child, your mother adores your face; your brothers and friends are all at the door."

alternates.speaker: the gopis
alternates.setting: The women of Braj, after Krishna has left, on missing him.
alternates.sanskrit: निसिदिन बरसत नैन हमारे। सदा रहति पावस ऋतु हम पै जब तें स्याम सिधारे॥
alternates.line: "Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes."
alternates.translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.
alternates.why: Tears for someone you miss are allowed.

verse.speaker: Kausalya
verse.setting: After lashing out at Dasharatha over Ram's exile, Kausalya apologises and explains what grief did to her.
verse.sanskrit: शोको नाशयते धैर्यं शोको नाशयते श्रुतम्। शोको नाशयते सर्वं नास्ति शोकसमो रिपुः॥
verse.line: Grief wears away your steadiness and your judgement. There is no enemy like it.
verse.translation: Grief destroys steadiness, grief destroys learning, grief destroys everything. There is no enemy like grief.
verse.why: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.
verse.misuse: Not a ban on grieving; a warning not to let sorrow make your decisions.

prasang.title: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasang.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.
prasang.story_hook: She said the words; then she saw her husband fold his hands to her.
prasang.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.

verse.for_you: Arjuna saw grief dry him up. Now Kausalya names the enemy. You feel it in the quiet flat. The steadiness of twelve years is gone. Let the quiet be the ground you stand on.
verse.try_today: Notice when grief makes a decision for you.
verse.scene_line: Kausalya speaks of grief destroying steadiness while you sit in the quiet flat.

why: spoken by a mother who has just seen what her grief made her say

verse.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 493
verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.listener: Mary Hale, whose father had just died
verse.setting: Condolence letter, 20 February 1900: a friend who has known many losses offers to carry hers.
verse.line: if it were possible to exchange grief, and had I a cheerful mind, I would exchange mine for your grief ever and always.
verse.translation: You have had shelter all your life. I was in the glare, burning and panting all the time. Now for a moment you have caught a glimpse of the other side. My life is made up of continuous blows like that, and hundred times worse, because of poverty, treachery, and my own foolishness! Pessimism! You will understand it, how it comes. Well, well, what shall I say to you, Mary? You know all the talks; only I say this and it is true — if it were possible to exchange grief, and had I a cheerful mind, I would exchange mine for your grief ever and always. Mother knows best.
verse.for_you: Yesterday grief was named as an enemy. Today someone offers to carry it with you, as if grief could be exchanged. Someone would carry it with you.
verse.try_today: Notice one small act of care you can offer yourself today.
verse.scene_line: Mary's friend offers to carry her grief, as you carry the quiet after Bruno.

verse.line: Your wisdom isn't gone. Grief has only put it to sleep for a while.
verse.translation: Your understanding, wise one, is beyond even the gods' reckoning. Grief has only put your wisdom to sleep, and I am here to wake it.
verse.for_you: Yesterday grief was named as an enemy. Today someone offers to carry it with you, as if grief could be exchanged. Someone would carry it with you. Grief has only put your wisdom to sleep. The quiet flat is the sound of that sleep. Your wisdom is still here, beyond even the gods.

why: Feelings come and go, bear them; your wisdom is asleep, not gone (Lakshmana to Rama).

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: How a householder becomes a 'world' for others.
verse.sanskrit: यन्मनुष्यान्वासयते यदेभ्योऽशनं ददाति तेन मनुष्याणामथ यत्पशुभ्यस्तृणोदकं विन्दति तेन पशूनां यदस्य गृहेषु श्वापदा वयाꣳस्या पिपीलिकाभ्य उपजीवन्ति तेन तेषां लोको
verse.line: Feed people, find water for animals; when even ants live off your home, you become a world for them.
verse.translation: By housing people and giving them food, he becomes a world for people. By finding grass and water for animals, he becomes a world for animals. When beasts, birds and even ants live off his house, he becomes a world for them.
verse.for_you: Yesterday grief was named. Today, the care you gave Bruno is still a world. His quiet is the space he made for you.
verse.scene_line: You sit in the quiet flat, and the ants still find their way.

why: the care reaches down to birds and ants
a household is seen as something many lives rest on

verse.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).

verse.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

prasang.title: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

story.title: Hanuman reaches Sita
story.story_hook: A ring fell out of the tree onto Sita's lap, and it had Ram's name on it.
story.summary: Sita, captive and threatened by Ravana, has nearly lost hope; only the guard Trijata has been kind. Hanuman drops Ram's ring from a tree, then tells her Ram's whole story. Sita says he has been her ship in a sea of separation; he gives her Ram's message that speaking of pain helps, but there is no one to tell, and asks her to wait a few days more.
story.lesson: When someone is near despair, a message that they are remembered can carry them.

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse.sanskrit: कहेहू तें कछु दुख घटि होई। काहि कहौं यह जान न कोई॥ तत्व प्रेम कर मम अरु तोरा। जानत प्रिया एकु मनु मोरा ॥
verse.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.
verse.why: When someone is near despair, a message that they are remembered can carry them.

prasang.story_hook: A ring fell out of the tree onto Sita's lap, and it had Ram's name on it.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
verse.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to stay steady when people and wealth come and go.
verse.sanskrit: मानसानां पुनर्योनिर्दुःखानां चित्तविभ्रमः / अनिष्टोपनिपातो वा तृतीयं नोपपद्यते
verse.line: Mental pain comes from two places: something you didn't want happened, or your mind is spinning. No third.
verse.translation: Sorrow of the mind has only two sources: a confused, wandering mind, or something unwanted happening to you. There is no third.
verse.why: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

prasang.title: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

verse.try_today: Notice if the flat is quiet or if your mind is wandering, and let the name of it be enough.

why: Two sources of the mind's pain (Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Ashma Gita))

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: Lecture 'Work and Its Secret', Los Angeles, 4 January 1900. On those who avoid pain by never loving.
verse.line: the man who never loves, who is hard and stony, escaping most of the miseries of life, escapes also its joys.
verse.translation: Therefore the man who never loves, who is hard and stony, escaping most of the miseries of life, escapes also its joys.
verse.why: Look after the means; keep the power to let go.

prasang.title: Work and its secret (Los Angeles, 1900)
prasang.summary: His greatest lesson, he says, was to attend to the means as much as the end. Most failures come from neglecting the means, and most sorrow from clinging to what is already failing. Weakness invites misery, yet a heart that refuses to love also loses life's joys.
prasang.lesson: Look after the means; keep the power to let go.

verse.sanskrit: चेतसा सर्वकर्माणि मयि संन्यस्य मत्परः । बुद्धियोगमुपाश्रित्य मच्चित्तः सततं भव ॥
verse.line: Inwardly hand all your work to the divine, hold it as your goal, and keep your mind on it.
verse.translation: Mentally resigning all actions to me, holding me as the highest, relying on the yoga of understanding, keep your mind always on me.
verse.why: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

prasang.title: Action with devotion: surrender
prasang.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.
prasang.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

verse.speaker: The ancestors (pitris)
verse.setting: Ending a long hymn, the ancestors stop asking for anything particular and hand the outcome to Shiva.
verse.sanskrit: विहारिन् ! विभो ! भक्तचेतोनिकेते शरण्यं किलैकान्ततस्त्वां व्रजामः । यथा नो भवेदत्र कल्याणमाशु तदेवाधुना देव ! शम्भो ! विधेहि ॥
verse.line: You who live in devotees' hearts: we come to you alone. Do whatever is truly good for us.
verse.translation: Dweller in the shrine of devotees' hearts, all-pervading one, we come to you alone for refuge. Do now, divine Shambhu, whatever will quickly bring us good here.

words.en: in the temple of devotee's mind

verse.why: You can hand over the outcome and still keep working, with devotion woven through.
verse.misuse: Handing over the outcome comes after the effort; it is not a reason to stop acting.

prasang.title: The ancestors' hymn to Shiva and his easy way
prasang.summary: Bewildered by Shiva's limitless form, the ancestors praise him and finally hand him the outcome: do whatever is truly good for us. Shiva tells them their work needs a mind joined to him, then gives an easy way: see him everywhere, even in a loving embrace, so devotion never lapses amid hard work.
prasang.lesson: You can hand over the outcome and still keep working, with devotion woven through.

story.title: Kunti watches her sons and daughter-in-law walk into exile
story.story_hook: She was too old to go with them. She stood at the gate and said one thing to her daughter-in-law, and then she wept.
story.summary: Kunti is too old for the forest, so Vidura will keep her in his house. She watches her five sons leave in deerskins, heads down, mocked by Duhshasana. Draupadi comes to take her leave in a single stained garment with her hair loose.
story.lesson: A parent's part, when the children must go, is to bless them truthfully and bear the waiting.
story.teaser: She was too old to go with them. She stood at the gate and said one thing to her daughter-in-law, and then she wept.

verse.speaker: Bharat
verse.setting: Bharat, urged by his teacher and mother to accept the throne, explains why he cannot.
verse.sanskrit: तुम्ह तौ देहु सरल सिख सोई। जो आचरत मोर भल होई॥ जद्यपि यह समुझत हउँ नीकें। तदपि होत परितोष न जी कें ॥
verse.line: I understand your advice perfectly. My heart still isn't at peace.
verse.translation: You give me simple advice, the kind that would do me good if I followed it. Though I understand it well, my heart is not at peace.
verse.why: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

prasang.title: Bharat refuses the throne
prasang.summary: After the funeral, Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya all urge Bharat to rule, as his father wished. Bharat says the advice is right and his heart still isn't at peace; the crown means nothing without Ram. He decides to go to the forest, admit his fault, and trust his brother to forgive.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone agreed the throne was his, and Bharat could not bring himself to sit on it.
prasang.lesson: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

verse.for_you: You understand that the flat is quiet now, and the advice that time heals does not bring your heart to rest. The silence of the room is not something you can simply understand your way out of. Peace will not arrive just because you know what you are missing.

verse.speaker: Kakbhushundi
verse.setting: Kakbhushundi, explaining to Garuda how people misjudge what they see.
verse.sanskrit: नयन दोष जा कहँ जब होई। पीत बरन ससि कहुँ कह सोई॥ जब जेहि दिसि भ्रम होई खगेसा। सो कह पच्छिम उयउ दिनेसा ॥ नौकारूढ़ चलत जग देखा। अचल मोह बस आपुहि लेखा॥ बालक भ्रमहिं न भ्रमहिं गृहादी। कहहिं परस्पर मिथ्याबादी ॥
verse.line: Diseased eyes see a yellow moon. From a moving boat, the shore seems to move.
verse.translation: When someone's eyes are diseased, he calls the moon yellow; when someone loses his bearings, he says the sun rose in the west. A man on a moving boat sees the world moving and, deluded, thinks himself still. Children spin round, not the houses, yet they call each other liars.
verse.why: Doubt is human; stay long enough in good company and it can lead somewhere better.

prasang.title: Garuda's doubt
prasang.summary: Garuda, Vishnu's own mount, frees Ram from a serpent-noose in battle and starts to doubt: how can God be bound? He goes to Narada, Brahma and Shiva, who sends him to an old crow, Kakbhushundi, saying doubts clear only with long time in good company. Kakbhushundi tells him no one has escaped delusion, desire, craving or anger; Garuda ends up grateful for the doubt that led him there.
prasang.story_hook: The great eagle Garuda flew to a crow to ask a question.
prasang.lesson: Doubt is human; stay long enough in good company and it can lead somewhere better.

verse.translation: For the one who knows, in whom all beings have become the self, what confusion, what sorrow can there be, seeing oneness everywhere?

verse.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Lectures and Discourses: Is Vedanta The Future Religion?, p. 127
verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: Lecture 'Is Vedanta the Future Religion?', San Francisco, 8 April 1900.
verse.line: There are mistakes but no sin; and in the long run everything is going to be all right.
verse.translation: These are what Vedanta has not to give. No book. No man to be singled out from the rest of mankind — "You are worms, and we are the Lord God!" — none of that. If you are the Lord God, I also am the Lord God. So Vedanta knows no sin. There are mistakes but no sin; and in the long run everything is going to be all right. No Satan — none of this nonsense. Vedanta believes in only one sin, only one in the world, and it is this: the moment you think you are a sinner or anybody is a sinner, that is sin. From that follows every other mistake or what is usually called sin. There have been many mistakes in our lives. But we are going on. Glory be unto us that we have made mistakes! Take a long look at your past life. If your present condition is good, it has been caused by all the past mistakes as well as successes. Glory be unto success! Glory be unto mistakes! Do not look back upon what has been done. Go ahead!

why: mistakes, not sin
Vedanta never calls you a worm

verse.line: If you can't keep your mind fixed yet, then reach for it through regular practice.
verse.translation: If you cannot fix your mind steadily on me, then seek to reach me by the yoga of practice, Dhananjaya.
verse.why: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.

prasang.title: Form or formless: which devotee is best, and the ways to reach him
prasang.summary: Krishna says devotion to a personal form is easier, then offers a ladder: fix your mind; if not, practise; if not, work for me; if not, let go of results. Letting go brings peace at once.
prasang.lesson: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.
